Non-rotating and perfectly round. One number, the mass, sets everything: horizon at r_s, photon sphere at 1.5 r_s, innermost stable orbit at 3 r_s.
Rotating (a = 0.9). Spin drags spacetime around with it: the horizon shrinks, an ergosphere appears, and orbits moving with the spin can survive much closer than those moving against it.
Ten solar masses, like the remnant of a massive star. Its horizon is only 30 km across; tides near it are extreme and its disk shines in X-rays at millions of kelvin.
6.5 billion solar masses, like M87* imaged in 2019. Its horizon is larger than our Solar System's planetary orbits, so an astronaut could cross it without feeling the tides.
The story's primordial black hole: six Earth masses packed inside a horizon about 10 cm across, spinning at a = 0.8. Almost no gas falls in, so its disk is faint.

Radio signals take 3 to 22 minutes to cross between Mars and Earth, depending on where the planets are. Every 26 months the Sun sits between them and blocks contact for about two weeks.
Leaving Mars takes about 4.1 km/s to reach low orbit, half of what leaving Earth takes. Its methane and oxygen propellant can be made on Mars from CO2 and water ice.
NASA's SEV concept: a pressurised rover that two astronauts can live in for up to two weeks, with suit ports on the back so they can step out without an airlock.

Landed in Jezero crater on 18 Feb 2021. Mass 1,025 kg, about 3 m long. Powered by an MMRTG: about 110 W from the heat of plutonium-238 decay. Its MOXIE experiment made the first oxygen on another planet, up to 12 g per hour.
First powered flight on another planet (19 Apr 2021). The air is about 1% as dense as Earth's, so its 1.2 m rotors spun at about 2,400 rpm. It flew 72 times.
A G2V main-sequence star, 1.39 million km across, surface about 5,772 K. It turns once every 25 days at the equator and 35 days near the poles.
Smallest planet: 4,879 km across. No real atmosphere, so its surface swings from about 430 °C by day to −180 °C at night. A year lasts 88 days.
Nearly Earth's size, but buried under a 92-bar CO2 atmosphere with sulfuric-acid clouds. The surface is about 465 °C, hotter than Mercury. It spins backwards.
The only world known to host life. 71% ocean. Its nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere scatters blue light; at night the cities glow.
3,474 km across, tidally locked to Earth. The dark maria are ancient lava plains; the bright highlands are heavily cratered crust. Relief here comes from LRO laser altimetry.

6,779 km across, with a thin 0.6 kPa CO2 atmosphere. Home of Olympus Mons (about 22 km high) and Valles Marineris (about 4,000 km long). Polar caps of water ice and CO2 frost. Relief from NASA's MOLA laser altimeter.
Largest planet: 11 Earths across, mostly hydrogen and helium. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries.
Its rings are mostly water ice, 280,000 km across but often only about 10 m thick. Saturn is less dense than water.
An ice giant tipped on its side (98° axial tilt). Methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light, giving it a cyan colour.
The windiest planet: supersonic winds up to about 2,100 km/h. Methane makes it blue. One orbit takes 165 years.
A metal-rich asteroid about 220 km across, perhaps the exposed core of a shattered protoplanet. NASA's Psyche spacecraft arrives in 2029.
A 490 m carbon-rich rubble pile, loosely held together by its own weak gravity. OSIRIS-REx brought 121.6 g of it to Earth in 2023.

The largest object in the asteroid belt, 940 km across, holding about a third of the belt's mass. NASA's Dawn found bright salt deposits in Occator crater from briny water below. (Shown with lunar textures as a stand-in.)
A dirty snowball a few km across. Near the Sun its ices sublimate: the blue ion tail is pushed straight away from the Sun by the solar wind, the curved dust tail trails along the orbit.
A 45 km crater that once held a lake. Its river delta is where Perseverance searched for signs of ancient life from 2021, and where the ARES-1 colony stands in 2189.
26.8 x 22.4 x 18.4 km, orbiting just 6,000 km above Mars, faster than Mars spins, so it rises in the west. Stickney crater is 9 km wide. (Shown 10x larger.)
The smaller moon, 15 x 12 x 10 km, smoothed by a thick layer of regolith. From Mars it looks like a bright star. (Shown 10x larger.)

ARES-1's orbital research station in a 1,400 km orbit: a 2.4 m survey telescope, power and propulsion element, habitation modules and a docking hub for landers from Jezero. It watches millions of stars for tiny changes in brightness. (Model: NASA Gateway; shown enlarged.)
In orbit since 2006 in a near-polar 255 x 320 km orbit. Its HiRISE camera resolves objects about 1 m across; it also relays rover data to Earth. (Shown enlarged.)
Light bends around it: the far side of the accretion disk appears over the top, an Einstein ring wraps beneath, and the approaching side of the disk shines brighter (Doppler beaming).
An ISA relay satellite placed in a high orbit in 2171 to collect PROJECT HORIZON's data. Its transmitter failed years ago, but its memory may still hold the expedition's last archive.
One of three observation pods Commander Varga's crew placed in stable orbits around HORIZON-1 in 2172. Its beacon still blinks every 40 seconds. (Not to scale.)

Ground-penetrating radar: ice-cemented regolith from 4.5 m down, about 35% ice by volume, perchlorate 0.6%.
Ground-penetrating radar: nearly clean ice from 1.1 m down, about 62% ice by volume, perchlorate 0.4%.
Ground-penetrating radar: shallow frost at 0.6 m, but only about 12% ice by volume, perchlorate 0.9%.
Grey spherules a few mm across: hematite concretions, like Opportunity's "blueberries". They form when groundwater deposits iron oxide.
Bright white veins: gypsum, hydrated calcium sulfate (CaSO4·2H2O), deposited by water flowing through cracks.
Green crystals: olivine, a volcanic mineral that water quickly breaks down. Where it survives, the rock stayed dry.
Probe telemetry: floor at 22 m, temperature −70 °C, steady within 1 °C day and night. Water ice detected on the floor. Radiation dose 3% of the surface.
Ares-0 descent stage, landed sol 1, 2161. Hull plate stencil: "HALVORSEN / OKONKWO / REYES / SATO". A crew patch is still taped inside the hatch.
Record 1 of 3: Ares-0 landed with four crew and 900 days of supplies. Their greenhouse failed in its first dust storm.
Record 2 of 3: "Sol 380. We are rationing water to two litres. The survey found ice, but we do not have the power to mine it." (T. Halvorsen)
Record 3 of 3: "Three of us will take the ascent vehicle. One seat is short. I'm staying with the survey data so the next crew won't have to start from nothing." (T. Halvorsen, sol 415)
